item.title: Hegseth calls impeachment push 'sabotage' in rare Pentagon press briefing
item.description:
Source: Yahoo Top Stories (World)
Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth struck a defiant tone in a Pentagon news briefing on Tuesday, a day after articles of impeachment were filed against him. Rep. Thomas Massie, a Republican from Kentucky, reintroduced the articles of impeachment on Monday, alleging that the embattled Pentagon chief had committed "high crimes and misdemeanors" and abused the power of his office by violating the War Powers Resolution, conducting military operations without congressional authorization and ordering unlawful military actions in several countries. Hegseth described the impeachment efforts as "a farce," stating: "None of these are high crimes or misdemeanors — they are partisan policy disagreements from people who want to politicize our military." He added, "That's what it is. Police disagreements. Not high crimes. Not misdemeanors. Not treason. Not bribery. Not the kinds of offenses the founders intended when they wrote the impeachment clause." While Hegseth did not mention Massie by name, he criticized the actions of a "disgruntled congressman" and said the "proper remedy" for a policy disagreement was legislation. "It's a political spectacle," Hegseth said. "A personal manifesto driven by ego and resentment. Time for one man's final days in Congress to try to do damage to this president." He added, "This is not patriotism. This is sabotage." Hegseth also said the resolution suggested the U.S. would punish its own military for carrying out their jobs. "Let's be clear about what this resolution actually does," he said. "It tells our enemies — Iran, the cartels, every adversary watching — that the United States will actually punish its own warriors and its own civilian leadership." In response, President Trump posted on Truth Social that Hegseth had earned an "'A' PLUS, PLUS, PLUS" for his defense against Massie. Trump described Hegseth as "perhaps the most popular and successful military official in the Country," adding, "Pete Hegseth should be praised, not Impeached. Congress, stand up for Pete!!!" The expected impeachment filing came as Congress returned to Washington, D.C. , to begin a lame-duck session following the historic rout that the GOP suffered in last week's midterm elections . Hegseth is facing intense political backlash over the United States' costly and unpopular war with Iran, which some top Republicans — including Trump — blame in part for the drubbing that cost them control of Congress. "Despite the absence of a declaration of war, specific statutory authorization, or a national emergency created by an attack upon the United States," Massie said in a speech on the House floor, "Secretary Hegseth knowingly executed and implemented unlawful orders to initiate war against a foreign nation." Massie said Hegseth "has demonstrated that he will remain a threat to the Constitution if allowed to remain in office, and has acted in a manner grossly incompatible with his duties and the rule of law." His actions thus "warrant impeachment and trial, removal from office and disqualification to hold and enjoy any office of honor, trust or profit under the United States," the Kentucky Republican said. Earlier, Trump told CNN at a White House press conference he would "stand by him," saying that he believes Massie "has a lot of hatred in his heart." Hegseth leaves a meeting of defense ministers in the Philippines on Oct. 28. Pool via Getty Images Massie — who in May lost his bid for reelection to Ed Gallrein, a Trump-backed challenger, in the GOP primary — first introduced articles of impeachment against Hegseth in September. But House Speaker Mike Johnson later canceled the final scheduled voting day before the midterm recess, delaying a vote. It's unclear whether an impeachment effort will succeed in the House, which is still under Republican control, but Massie told ABC News that he's "confident there will be enough GOP defectors for it to pass." To do so, the resolution requires a simple majority, meaning that just three Republicans would need to vote with all Democrats to prevail. A vote could come as soon as this week. Trump has repeatedly insisted that he is not considering replacing his Pentagon chief, at least not yet. "No, I think he's doing a very good job," Trump told reporters last week. The president also said he was unaware of a report that Hegseth has been quietly angling to fill the U.S. Senate seat that will be vacated by Tennessee GOP Sen. Marsha Blackburn, who was elected as the state's next governor. "I think he's doing a very good job, and I actually think he'd be very popular if he did that. But I haven't heard that at all," Trump said when asked if he would want the defense secretary to fill Blackburn's seat. CBS News , however, reported last week that Trump "has been asking advisers" whether he should stay or go. Hegseth, a former Fox News host who has served as defense secretary since January 2025, has been Trump's most visible cheerleader for the Iran war, which the U.S. and Israel initiated in February and which has led to surging oil prices. He has also been among the advisers urging Trump to restart the war. He and Adm. Brad Cooper, the head of U.S. Central Command, have supported a return to major combat operations against Iran during recent briefings on military options, the Wall Street Journal reported on Nov. 6, while Vice President JD Vance and special envoy Steve Witkoff have pushed for diplomacy to end the conflict. The U.S. Capitol building is seen in Washington, D.C., on Nov. 4. Kevin Carter/Getty Images Trump acknowledged on Nov. 4 that the Iran war had partly contributed to the midterm election rout that handed Democrats control of Congress. Vance was unequivocal. "The real reason we lost is obvious to almost everyone," Vance wrote in a lengthy post on X . "The reason we lost is the war." The vice president did not call out Hegseth by name. But other Republicans did. Sen. Thom Tillis, a Republican from North Carolina, told CBS News that Hegseth faces "a reckoning." "He is one of the reasons why we don't have the funding or guarantee for defense that we need," Tillis said on election night. "I think after the election, we need to determine whether or not he's the best person to bring those needs to Congress." Tillis, who voted to confirm Hegseth last year, recently called on Trump to fire him. "I have never witnessed more inept management of the brave men and women who serve our country," Tillis wrote in a scathing assessment of Hegseth on X in September. "He is intimidated by competence and retreats to ginning up culture wars instead of soberly attending to the vital work of our national defense and the health and well-being of our fighting force. I urge the President to find a new leader at the Pentagon who will retain and empower our military talent rather than diminish it." Rep. James Comer of Kentucky, the Republican chairman of the House Oversight Committee, said on Nov. 6 that "there's a lot of questions about Hegseth." "We have no idea what the strategy is moving forward in Iran," Comer told NewsNation . "No one's happy about Iran." A fire burns at an oil depot in Tehran, Iran, on March 8 after U.S. and Israeli attacks. Hassan Ghaedi/Anadolu via Getty Images When Democrats take control of both the House and Senate next year, they will have the ability to call for hearings and launch investigations into virtually any aspect of the Trump administration — and Hegseth's handling of the military is high on their list. "In the majority, one of the first things we're gonna do is run Pete Hegseth out of town," Rep. Hakeem Jeffries of New York, the minority leader who is poised to become House speaker in January, said at a rally last month . Hegseth, for his part, has remained defiant. In a 5-and-a-half-minute video posted to X on Nov. 5, Hegseth defended the Iran war, touted changes he's implemented as Pentagon chief ("We ended the weird and the woke") and praised Trump's leadership while dismissing Massie's impeachment pursuit. "A disgruntled, defeated congressman along with all his Democrat allies has dropped sham impeachment articles against yours truly," Hegseth said. "It didn't work with President Trump and it won't work with me." item.title: Russia, Ukraine and the U.S. meet for talks as Trump says war can 'end soon'
item.description:
Source: Yahoo Top Stories (World)
American, Ukrainian and Russian representatives gathered in Abu Dhabi on Tuesday for their latest round of trilateral peace talks, with President Donald Trump's administration seeking a diplomatic breakthrough after 1,721 days of Moscow's full-scale invasion of its neighbor. Trump -- who came to office vowing to end the war within 24 hours -- has thus far been unable to force a breakthrough. His chief negotiating envoys, Steve Witkoff and Trump's son-in-law, Jared Kushner, are leading the U.S. delegation in Abu Dhabi this week. On Monday, Trump struck a positive tone when discussing the coming meeting. "They talk about wars, Ukraine and Russia. And by the way, we're having a very good conversation about that in Abu Dhabi," the president said. "Ukraine and Russia are tired of fighting. They're tired of seeing dead young soldiers," Trump added. Rustem Umerov Via Telegram/via Reuters - PHOTO: Members of the Ukrainian, U.S. and Russian peace talks delegations meet in Abu Dhabi, United Arab Emirates, on Nov. 10, 2026. Ukraine must 'unblock' Patriot missile delivery, Zelenskyy says after deadly strikes A source in Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy's office told ABC News that Kyiv's delegation is led by Rustem Umerov, the head of Ukraine's Foreign Intelligence Service and its lead representative in previous rounds of talks . Among those accompanying him are Kyrylo Budanov, the head of Zelenskyy's office, and Davyd Arakhamia, the head of Zelenskyy's party in the Ukrainian parliament. The Russian delegation is led by Kremlin aide Vladimir Medinsky, Kremlin spokesperson Dmitry Peskov said. Also attending are Kremlin official Yuri Ushakov, the head of Russia's foreign military intelligence agency, Igor Kostyukov, and Sergei Ryabkov, the deputy foreign minister, Peskov said. The first U.S.-brokered trilateral meeting was held in Geneva in February 2026, but this year has seen little diplomatic progress, with both camps still far apart on key issues. The negotiations have secured some prisoner-of-war exchanges and short-lived, localized ceasefires. Russian Foreign Minister Sergey Lavrov said on Monday that this week's talks will put "security issues concerning Russia, Ukraine and the region as a whole" at the top of the agenda. The participants would also work toward "agreeing on principles that could be approved following consultations on a comprehensive settlement of the conflict in Ukraine," Lavrov said. Zelenskyy said Monday that he had spoken with European Commission President Ursula von Der Leyen ahead of the talks. Both the French and German foreign ministers also said they would be participating in the Abu Dhabi meetings, though Peskov maintained that the talks would remain trilateral in format. Dan Bashakov/AP Photo - PHOTO: An man walks past a heavily damaged kindergarten building and a debris-strewn courtyard following a missile attack on a residential area in Kyiv, on Nov. 7, 2026. 'It's not supportive': Ukraine's Zelenskyy laments lack of US assistance in war with Russia A statement posted to the Ukrainian presidential website said Kyiv "is doing everything to ensure that the trilateral format delivers results." Delegation head Umerov, meanwhile, said in a post to Telegram on Tuesday morning that Kyiv's team is prioritizing "ending hostilities, reliable post-war security guarantees, economic recovery and development of Ukraine, and humanitarian measures." With the war approaching its fifth anniversary, the two combatants appear far apart on a potential settlement. Russian President Vladimir Putin has repeatedly rejected U.S.-Ukrainian proposals for a ceasefire under which a final settlement could be negotiated. Moscow is demanding that Ukraine withdraw from four contested regions -- Donetsk, Luhansk, Zaporizhzhia and Kherson -- the Kremlin claimed to have annexed in September 2022, after referendums that the international community largely refused to recognize. Putin also wants Ukraine permanently barred from NATO and to face limits on the size and capabilities of its military. Zelenskyy has said Ukraine cannot agree to any deal that does not include concrete security guarantees from the U.S. and other NATO allies to protect against renewed Russian aggression. Kyiv, Zelenskyy said, must also retain the right to constitute its own armed forces and choose its own future security arrangements, including membership of NATO. The Ukrainian leader has refused Russian demands to cede territory not controlled by Moscow's forces. Gavriil Grigorov/Pool Sputnik via EPA/Shutterstock - PHOTO: Russian President Vladimir Putin attends a meeting with special envoy Steve Witkoff at the Constantine Palace in Strelna, a suburb of St. Petersburg, Russia, October 21, 2026. Witkoff lauds 'humanitarian' Putin as Russia releases detained American Since Trump returned to office, U.S.-Ukrainian ties have at times been fraught. The president has repeatedly pressured Zelenskyy to make concessions to Moscow in pursuit of a peace deal. Trump has described Zelenskyy at times as a "dictator" and criticized Kyiv for delaying planned elections, which constitutionally cannot be held while the country is under martial law. Trump has suspended U.S. financial and military aid to Ukraine, instead demanding that other NATO allies purchase American arms intended for Ukraine's use. Kyiv has repeatedly appealed to the U.S. to provide more ammunition for its Patriot surface-to-air missile systems in particular, the systems key to Ukrainian efforts to blunt escalating Russian drone and ballistic missile strikes. In March, Trump threatened to expand sanctions and tariffs on Russia in a bid to push Moscow to the negotiating table. Ultimately Trump failed to do so, and in the lead-up to this month's midterm elections struck a deal with Putin to import cargoes of Russian diesel -- a move that prompted criticism from domestic opponents, foreign allies and Kyiv. Trump told CBS News' "60 Minutes" program on Sunday that he still believes an agreement to end Russia's full-scale invasion is possible. "I believe that that war is going to end and it's going to end soon. And the only reason it's going to end is because of me," Trump said. Andrew Harnik/Getty Images - PHOTO: President Donald Trump speaks during an event in the Oval Office of the White House, November 5, 2026 in Washington 'The blockade is complete': Locals flee occupied south Ukraine as hunger deepens Trump also appeared to imply that he was open to changes in Ukraine's borders as part of a peace agreement, saying that the country will end up with "a little bit different shape Ukraine." Trump said the enmity between Putin and Zelenskyy was the prime obstacle to a deal: "There's tremendous hatred," he said. Asked whether that sentiment is understandable coming from Zelenskyy, given that his country was invaded, Trump said it is, but also suggested that Ukraine had disrespected Russia during an initial meeting. "Well, it is, but when they had their first meeting, there was great disrespect shown to Russia. So I'm not going to say," Trump said. Asked if he thought Putin was stringing him along, Trump replied, "Oh, I don't think so." A U.S. official told ABC News during a briefing on Monday that negotiators were "cautiously optimistic" ahead of the talks in Abu Dhabi, though framed the meeting as a jumping off point for more complex negotiations to end the war. "While both parties remain skeptical of the other party's intentions, we do see promising signs as the mediator, and we're going to work to keep pushing to build the areas of common ground so that we can work to a conclusion," the U.S. official said. Trump's comments and conduct have deepened concerns in Ukraine that the president wants the victims of the war, rather than the aggressors, to pay the price for peace, Oleksandr Merezhko -- a member of the Ukrainian parliament and the chair of the body's foreign affairs committee -- told ABC News. Sergei Supinsky/AFP via Getty Images - PHOTO: A passerby walks past a Ukrainian flag displayed on a large monitor during a power outage in the centre of Kyiv on Nov. 7, 2026. Pentagon inspector general declines to investigate Starlink disruptions in Ukraine Merezhko said he has "absolutely no hopes" for this week's meetings in Abu Dhabi, beyond possible new deals to exchange prisoners of war. "There can't be any tangible result because Putin keeps insisting on his absurd demands which, in reality, mean surrender for Ukraine," he said. "Putin's goal is to imitate negotiations to avoid sanctions from Trump. But he has absolutely no intent to negotiate with a goal to reach a concrete result," Merezhko suggested. "His ultimate goal is not a ceasefire or a compromise; his goal is subjection of Ukraine and installment in Kyiv of a Russian puppet regime." Both Russian and American officials have said that the Abu Dhabi talks will include discussions on broader European security arrangements. That "seems to be new," said Samuel Charap, a senior political scientist at RAND who has advocated for talks. Still, Charap told ABC News, "They‘re not going to come to some radically more ambitious agreement given there hasn’t been any conversation for the past nine months." Yulia Morozova/Reuters - PHOTO: A supporter of the Russian Communist Party holds a pro-war leaflet during a rally in central Moscow, Russia, on Nov. 7, 2026. First lady Melania Trump says she brokered 'temporary' ceasefire in Ukrainian town Putin launched the invasion in February 2022 with the intention of dismembering Ukraine and installing a pliant government in Kyiv. The "special military operation," as the Kremlin termed the assault, marked the latest chapter in Moscow's decades-long effort to retain influence over Kyiv and undermine Ukraine's relations with the European Union and NATO. What the Kremlin intended as a short campaign has now lasted longer than either World War I or the Soviet Union's confrontation with Nazi Germany in World War II, known in Russia as Great Patriotic War. Russian officials routinely describe the war with Ukraine as a direct contest with the NATO alliance, whose constituent nations rallied to support Ukraine military and financially, added two new members -- Sweden and Finland -- and sought to increase collective military spending to meet the Russian threat. Fierce fighting continues all along the 745-mile frontline. The invasion quickly devolved into a bloody war of attrition, with Russian units edging forward -- at massive cost, according to figures published by the Ukrainian military and broadly supported by Western intelligence assessments -- along the contact line in parts of eastern and southeastern Ukraine. This year has seen significant Ukrainian counterattacks in the contested Dnipropetrovsk, Donetsk and Zaporizhzhia regions, liberating hundreds of miles of occupied territory, according to commanders in Kyiv. Andriy Andriyenko/Ukrainian 65 Mechanized brigade - PHOTO: In this photo provided by Ukraine's 65th Mechanized Brigade press service, recruits take an oath on the frontline in the Zaporizhzhia region, Ukraine, on Nov. 8, 2026. 'The basement saved me': Frontline Ukrainian city under fire amid US peace push Meanwhile, both Russia and Ukraine have expanded their long-range strike campaigns through the course of 2026. Each night, hundreds and sometimes thousands of drones and missiles cross the shared border heading in both directions, with Kyiv and Moscow both among the regular targets. The number of civilian casualties is steadily creeping up as a result, particularly among Ukrainians. Overnight into Tuesday, Ukraine's air force said Russia launched 162 drones, of which 96 were jet-powered, and one ballistic missile into the country. The air force said that 135 drones, of which 70 were jet-powered, were shot down or otherwise suppressed. Impacts were reported across 19 locations, the air force said. Russia's Defense Ministry, meanwhile, said its forces downed at least 155 Ukrainian drones overnight. AB C News' Vi c toria Beaule, Oleksiy Pshemyskyi, Natalia Kushnir, Tanya Stukalova, Anna Sergeeva, Shannon K. Kington and Mi c helle Stoddart c ontributed to this report. This article originally appeared on Good Morning America at https://abcnews.com/International/russia-ukraine-us-meet-abu-dhabi-talks-trump/story?id=137970621

item.title: The midterms aren't quite over: Lauren Boebert's reelection bid among key uncalled races
item.description:
Source: Yahoo Top Stories (World)
The dust has almost settled on the Democratic Party's 2026 midterm landslide — almost . It's clear that Democrats won sweeping victories in the U.S. House, Senate and statehouses nationwide . But some key races remain too close to call, including Senate brawls in deep-red Mississippi and Alaska; Rep. Lauren Boebert's reelection battle in Colorado; and other nail-biter House contests across the South. Here's the latest on how many seats Democrats have won so far — and where things stand in all of the unresolved races. How many Senate seats did Democrats win? Democrats came into the midterms needing a net gain of four seats to win back the Senate. To do that, they had to defend a handful of potentially vulnerable swing-state seats while also flipping at least a few seats in historically red states. That's exactly what happened. Republican efforts to flip blue seats in Michigan, Georgia, Minnesota and New Hampshire all came up well short. Meanwhile, Democrats secured victories to flip seven GOP-held seats in Maine, Texas, South Carolina, Ohio, North Carolina, Iowa and Kansas. Only two incumbent Republican senators in races that drew significant attention were able to win reelection: Florida's Ashley Moody and Nebraska's Pete Ricketts. As it stands, Democrats will enter 2027 with at least 54 seats in the Senate . They have already gained seven seats to give themselves, at minimum, a four-seat majority. Their majority could grow to six if the two remaining undecided races in Alaska and Mississippi go their way. Where things stand in the undecided Senate races Both races are extremely close, with no clear indication of when they might be decided. In Mississippi , Democrat Scott Colom's lead over Republican incumbent Cindy Hyde-Smith had grown to 2,536 votes as of Monday evening, according to the Associated Press . Outstanding absentee ballots in the race must be received by Tuesday in order to be counted, according to Mississippi state law. Colom's lead — which stood at just 65 votes on Election Day — has widened gradually in the days since. Even though 97% of the vote is in, AP has yet to call the race because the gap between Colom and Hyde-Smith remains narrow — just 0.27% of all ballots cast. Alaska's ranked choice voting system means it could take significantly longer for a winner to be declared. As it stands, Democrat Mary Peltola holds a lead of 637 votes over Republican incumbent Dan Sullivan, with 74% of ballots counted. The state is expected to have counted nearly all ballots by Nov. 13, with the last remaining votes tallied by Nov. 18. The wait for a final result could become extended if neither Peltola nor Sullivan receives more than 50% of the total first-choice votes. That would trigger a count of ranked choice votes to determine the winner. Under Alaska law, the ranked choice tally cannot begin until Nov. 18, which means a winner wouldn't be declared until two full weeks after Election Day. How many House seats did Democrats win? So far, Democrats have won 254 U.S. House seats — far more than the 218 they needed for a majority. That includes 44 red-to-blue flips. Democrats' 13-point victory in the House popular vote (so far) has been the largest in any midterm since 1974. Where things stand in the undecided House races On Monday afternoon, incumbent GOP Rep. Mario Diaz-Balart of western Miami defeated Democratic challenger Nicole Locklin by about 1,700 votes in Florida's 26th Congressional District. Incumbent GOP Rep. Michael Baumgartner also won a tight race Monday in Washington's 5th Congressional District. Another 18 U.S. House races remain unresolved. Two of them are in Louisiana, which holds open, nonpartisan "jungle primaries" on Election Day, then sends the top two finishers to a Dec. 12 runoff if no one gets a majority of the vote. One Democrat and one Republican will now go head-to-head next month in Louisiana's 5th and 6th Congressional Districts . California also has a nonpartisan jungle-primary system where members of the same party can advance to the general election. Officials are still counting ballots in California's 4th and 7th Districts , where only Democrats are competing. Of the remaining 14 races, Democrats lead in five. In Colorado's 4th Congressional District — long considered one of the state's safest Republican seats — GOP firebrand Lauren Boebert trails Democrat Eileen Laubacher, a retired rear admiral in the Navy, by more than 3,000 votes with just 2% of the vote left to count . After a close 2022 reelection fight in her previous district, Boebert switched to the 4th District for her 2024 campaign and won by about 11 percentage points. Colorado counties have until Nov. 13 to count ballots and upload final results. Right now, Laubacher's lead is too big to trigger an automatic recount. Democrats' next-largest lead is in central Florida's 9th Congressional District , where incumbent Democrat Darren Soto — who was targeted by GOP redistricting efforts — leads Republican challenger Dan Green by roughly 1,500 votes with more than 99% of the vote counted. The state of Florida has announced there will not be a recount in the 9th District because Soto's lead falls outside recount requirements. Soto is expected to win. Democrats' other leads are in Tennessee's 4th Congressional District , Minnesota's 1st Congressional District and North Carolina's 5th Congressional District . The margins in these races are in the 100- to 300-vote range. A recount is likely in Minnesota . Republicans lead in the other 9 unresolved races. Two of the closest are in Florida. Republican Ryan Elijah leads Democrat Bale Dalton by about 1,600 votes in Florida's 7th Congressional District — enough to avoid a recount under Sunshine State law. Meanwhile, Miami-Dade County election officials began a machine recount Monday in Florida's 27th Congressional District , where Republican Rep. María Elvira Salazar leads Democratic challenger Eliott Rodriguez by 1,090 votes, or 0.44 percentage points. That's within Florida's automatic half-point threshold. Nearly all of the other uncalled races where Republicans lead feature incumbent GOP lawmakers fending off strong challenges in reliably red areas: North Carolina's 3rd, 7th and 10th Districts ; South Carolina's 2nd District ; California's 23rd District ; and Alaska's only congressional district . The Western states are still waiting on big batches of mail ballots; the Eastern states have mostly finished counting. Republicans' only remaining pickup opportunity is Maine's 2nd Congressional District , where a conservative Democrat retired — and where former GOP Gov. Paul LePage now leads Matt Dunlap, the progressive state auditor, by more than 5,000 votes with just 2% left to count. A ranked-choice vote count will continue in the state despite Dunlap conceding to LePage on Nov. 5. How many governorships did Democrats win? Republican governors have outnumbered their Democratic counterparts for the last 15 years straight (and for 26 of the last 30 years overall). That's given Republicans more opportunities to experiment with new policy ideas, approve congressional maps, influence election procedures, fill Senate vacancies and build executive experience. But this year, Democrats have reversed the "governor gap," flipping five governorships in Iowa, Texas, Ohio, Nevada and Georgia to bring their total to 29 — the party's first gubernatorial majority since 2011. Where things stand in the undecided governor's races Kansas is anything but a blue state; since 1940, it has voted Republican in every presidential election but one — Lyndon B. Johnson's 1964 landslide. But the Sunflower State has elected two Democratic women governors in recent years: Kathleen Sebelius (2003-2009) and term-limited incumbent Laura Kelly (2019-2027). State Sen. Cindy Holscher is seeking to become the third. Holscher leads Republican Ty Masterson, the president of the state Senate, by more than 7,500 votes with nearly all of the ballots counted. Holscher declared victory on Nov. 4, saying that "the people of Kansas made their voices heard, and I'm deeply honored by the trust Kansans placed in me to serve as your next governor." But the race won't be officially over until all 105 Kansas counties complete a legally mandated close-race audit. Masterson said last week that he wouldn't concede before the audit was done. A source close to the Republican senator told the Kansas City Star that Masterson "did not plan to pursue an additional recount and would accept the results if Holscher's narrow win was finalized." Counties will certify their results on Nov. 15. In Alaska , three Republicans and a Democrat are running to replace Republican Gov. Mike Dunleavy. Democratic candidate Jonathan Kreiss-Tomkins is currently leading, with 49.6% of the vote. Republican Bernadette Wilson is in second, with 29.2% of the vote, with fellow GOP candidates Dave Bronson and Treg Taylor further behind. 76% of the vote has been counted. Alaska will proceed to a ranked-choice count if Kreiss-Tomkins doesn't clear 50% of the vote, but "preliminary ballot data shows that Wilson did not receive enough [ranked-choice] support to move ahead of the Democrat," according to the Anchorage Daily News . How many state legislatures did Democrats win? Democrats' gains were also seen at the state level. They flipped more than 500 state legislative seats across the country and turned a total of 12 legislative chambers blue. That includes three states where they flipped both chambers: Arizona, New Hampshire and Wisconsin. After Election Day's results, Democrats will control the House, Senate and governorship in Arizona for the first time since 1966. Democrats also secured a "trifecta" in Wisconsin. They'll hold both legislative chambers in New Hampshire, but the governorship in the Granite State will remain in Republican hands. Democrats regained trifectas in Minnesota, Michigan and Pennsylvania by clinching majorities in the lone GOP-led chamber in their states. They flipped a single chamber in Georgia, North Carolina and Texas, ensuring that Democratic governors in those states won't face unified Republican opposition within their state legislatures. Where things stand in the undecided state legislative races As of Monday evening, only three state legislative chambers — the North Carolina Senate and both chambers in Alaska — remained undecided, according to the AP. item.title: Hakeem Jeffries is poised to become House speaker. Some Dems want much more.
item.description:
Source: Yahoo Top Stories (World)
Hakeem Jeffries' supporters don't just want him to win — they want him to win big. The massive Democratic House victory last week has transformed what might have otherwise been a fraught effort for the sitting minority leader to secure the speaker's gavel , where a smaller majority could have empowered a tightknit block of hard-left holdouts. Now a broader group is intent on sending a message. "The people want to see unity," Rep. Troy Carter of Louisiana said in an interview. "They don't want to see fighting. They don't want to see infighting. They want to see the level of togetherness to advance an agenda." The good feelings surrounding Democrats' House gains have quieted the debate about the leadership of the caucus, however large it might be. As counting continues and operatives hold out hope for 260 seats — the largest majority for any party since 1993 — progressive activists continue to call for an alternative to Jeffries. While no sitting or incoming lawmaker has announced outright opposition, several who ran on populist economic platforms are withholding endorsements. "I want to see who the other options are and what their agendas are, so that we can make sure that it aligns with the needs of my congressional district," said Rep.-elect LaKesha Womack of North Carolina. On Capitol Hill, Jeffries' allies aren't fretting about the ultimate outcome — he can afford at least three dozen defections — but his allies are now working to unify Democrats ahead of a nominating vote next week and an official tally on the House floor in early January. "The American people want us to focus in on issues of affordability," Rep. Jim McGovern of Massachusetts, the incoming Rules Committee chair, said in an interview. "That's what I heard: affordability, affordability, affordability. So let's get on with the business of electing Hakeem as speaker, and let's focus in on what this election was all about." The chaotic past four years of GOP rule are hanging over the vote. Hamstrung by relatively tiny majorities, GOP leaders struggled to keep unruly factions in step — often resulting in dramatic confrontations. In 2023, a group of discontented Republicans voted out a speaker for the first time, putting the deposed Kevin McCarthy into the history books. Many Democrats said they are intent on setting the tone early that this majority will be functional and productive, not constantly racked by factional warfare. "I don't believe that we can have the kind of acrimony that we had under Kevin McCarthy and the Republicans," Rep.-elect Dan Koh of Massachusetts told reporters Sunday. "We need to learn from MAGA. … We need to get to the bottom of [President Donald] Trump's corruption and lower costs for people. We can't have months and months of acrimony." Jeffries boasts strong backing around the caucus, with power bases in the Congressional Black Caucus, which is projected to have more than 60 members next term, and the New Democrat Coalition, which is tracking toward more than 140 members. While there is overlap between those two groups and there could be defections, support from these two groups alone already puts Jeffries close to the 218 votes he would need in January. Plenty of top progressives are endorsing Jeffries, too. Rep. Greg Casar of Texas, the Congressional Progressive Caucus chair, is voting for him, as is the group's influential former chair, Rep. Pramila Jayapal of Washington. Rep. Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez of New York, perhaps the best-known face of the party's leftist wing, is also backing Jeffries and whipped out a whiteboard on a recent livestream to explain to her massive social-media following how the speaker election works. Not everyone is on board. A handful of new members, many but not all of whom are progressive, reaffirmed this weekend that they are as yet uncommitted to Jeffries. "I have a lot to consider," moderate Rep.-elect Zack Mullock of New Jersey said Sunday. "But it'll be an important decision that I'm going to talk to a lot of people who know a lot more than I do." Outside critics are hoping the noncommittals mean there's an opening to block Jeffries' ascension — or at least win concessions. Some leading progressives are framing the upcoming votes as a chance to resolve, or at least talk through, certain internally divisive issues before Democrats enter the majority. Rep. Ro Khanna of California cited "Medicare for All" health care policy and the U.S. relationship with Israel as particular flashpoints. "It's a healthy process to have that conversation," he said. "I think we will advance some of those policies that people voted for, and I'm part of those conversations." Jeffries said Monday he would be having plenty of personal conversations in the coming days. "I'm going to work hard to talk to every single member about what we've been able to do together over the last two years, and what the opportunities are for us to do together in the next two years, to deliver upon the dramatic change that the American people so decisively voted for," he said at a news conference. The members of the new Congress, both incumbent and incoming, will vote on a speaker nomination next week, which requires only a simple majority of Democrats. The tougher test is on the floor in January, where a speaker must win a majority of all 435 members. One recent benchmark is the backlash Rep. Nancy Pelosi of California faced after Democrats retook the majority in 2018, in the middle of Trump's first term. After being elected speaker with zero internal opposition in 2007 and 2009, 32 Democrats opposed her comeback in the caucus vote, and 15 ultimately voted for another candidate or recorded themselves as "present" on the floor — barely allowing her to eke through . But the caucus largely united behind Pelosi as she subsequently battled with Trump, and Rep. Jim Clyburn of South Carolina — who was No. 3 leader under Pelosi — said it was not important that every Democrat be in lockstep. "I don't know why everybody thinks you got to be unanimous," he said. "You can have unity and not be unanimous." Mia McCarthy contributed to this report. item.title: Inside James Gunn's shock DC ouster: Executive tensions and a David Ellison visit
item.description:
Source: Yahoo Top Stories (World)
DC Studios heads James Gunn and Peter Safran were feeling pretty secure under the new Skydance regime. After surviving a merger that claimed the jobs of celebrated Warner Bros. heads Mike De Luca and Pam Abdy, the duo were basking in the modest success of Clayface , a horror movie released Oct. 21 that passed $100 million globally on a $44 million budget. There was even talk of doing more spooky, slimmed-down DC movies. More from The Hollywood Reporter Six Hollywood Consequences of Tuesday's Democratic Blockbuster Chuck Lorre Talks David Ellison Optimism, Scientology and the Perks (Really!) of Working for Roseanne Barr Ynon Kreiz, the Intense, Kite Surfing CEO Who Thrives When His Back Is Against the Wall Gunn had also wrapped production on Man of Tomorrow , his sequel to Superman that is heading for a July 2027 release, and sources say he was in the midst of writing a third installment as part of plan to make a trilogy and release a Superman movie every two years, maybe even morphing the franchise into a Justice League teamup. Then came Friday, Nov. 6, when Skydance co-CEOs David Ellison and Ynon Kreiz arrived at Gunn and Safran’s offices on the Warner Bros. lot in Burbank. There, according to sources, the DC heads were told that despite previous assurances they would be part of the new Skydance mega-studio, Ellison and Kreiz had a change of plans. And now, after four years as two of the most visible faces in comic book films and TV, they were out . And their replacement was surprising. It wasn’t a splashy C-suiter or an exec recently ousted amid Hollywood consolidation. It was Jeremy Latcham, a mild-mannered producer who was once a key member of Marvel Studios’ exec team before moving to Texas to go independent. An occasional foray into big-budget moviemaking such as Dungeons & Dragons: Honor Among Thieves notwithstanding, Latcham was focusing on inspirational movies such as the Wright Brothers feature Flyer , for the faith-focused studio Wonder Project, where he also helped make House of David , a TV show about the Biblical figure. The producer is known to be vocal about his Christian faith and his desire to make uplifting projects. “I had this nagging feeling that I needed to do more movies that had deeper meaning to me,” Latcham said of Wonder Project during an appearance on the Bible Bros podcast while promoting the Nate Bargatze comedy The Breadwinner . “Let’s be the HBO for the faith and family audience. Let’s try to make movies and television shows that restore faith in things worth believing in.” In a twist, Latcham was instrumental in Gunn’s rise, advocating for the niche director’s hiring on Marvel Studios’ Guardians of the Galaxy , which turned Gunn into an A-list filmmaker who commands 8-figure paydays for his directing work. One insider indicated the exec shuffle had been in the works since early fall and had been precipitated by a reachout to Latcham from Josh Greenstein, who co-chairs the Skydance Motion Picture Group with Dana Goldberg. The two first worked together nearly 20 years ago when Latcham was a rising Marvel exec and Greenstein was in the marketing department at Paramount, the studio that released Iron Man and Iron Man 2 . They teamed again when Greenstein was at Sony and made Spider-Man: Homecoming with Marvel. Sources point to several points of tension between DC’s Gunn and Safran and Skydance’s Greenstein and Goldberg. Before Skydance’s acquisition, Gunn and Safran reported directly to Warner Bros. CEO David Zaslav; their contracts stipulated they would maintain that kind of direct reporting structure in the event of a change of leadership, in this case Ellison. That set up a chafing with Greenstein and Goldberg, who are trying to consolidate all production of motion pictures under their leadership. Gunn and Safran, meanwhile, were accustomed to having strong control over every aspect of the rollout of DC products. “They had the final word on movies, TV shows, and animation,” says one insider. They were not about to get layered in the reporting structure, multiple sources add. Another point of tension: sources say the DC heads were not forthcoming or were slow in sharing plans, slate details and footage with the Skydance movie heads. In the end, Greenstein and Goldberg prevailed and new hire Latcham will report to them. Another insider is more blunt in the assessment. Ellison never wanted DC to report directly to him in the first place and did not have time for studio politics, such as posturing between division heads. And then there was the matter of DC’s financials. The movies released were not great for business, while Supergirl was just a disaster , in the eyes of the new regime. Even Superman , which grossed $618 million worldwide and was profitable, did not net out, or have the kind of pop culture impact, in the way that kind of movie should, Skydance‘s thinking went. Latcham’s rise to the top of DC Studios began 22 years ago, during a very different era for superhero movies. In 2004, he was working as an assistant at Endeavor when exec David Maisel left to lead Marvel Studios as president and hired him as his assistant at the upstart studio. Latcham is said have been surprised and underwhelmed when he showed up to Marvel’s modest Santa Monica Blvd. offices to discover it wasn’t yet a real a studio, but rather an outfit for giving script notes to Hollywood studios making licensed movies based on Marvel characters. But a year and a half later, Maisel orchestarted a deal for Marvel to finance its own movies, starting with Iron Man . As Latcham shot through the ranks at Marvel, moving on to become Kevin Feige’s assistant and then his right-hand man, he was known for musing aloud about if his grandparents would like their movies. In other words, he asked, “Would this movie resonate with everyday people beyond Hollywood?” while walking the thin line in servicing what superfans would love. Sources affectionately describe Latcham as a down the middle shooter whose goal is to make hits for the masses and get people into movie theaters. If Gunn was the guy to deliver f-bombs and lesser known characters, Latcham is the guy to deliver what’s more in line with Ellison’s broader tastes, say multiple sources. Known as a family man who doesn’t care about the trappings of Hollywood, Latcham is expected to split time between Los Angeles and his home in Texas, where he lives with his wife and daughter, as well as his parents, who live on their property. He is not the kind of producer who has extensive relationships with agents, which may be detriment or benefit, depending on who you talk to. He is expected to be very hands on producer who likes to spend time on sets. Gunn and Safran will still have direct links to the studio, just less control. Safran is a prolific producer with a long relationship with Warner Bros. through The Conjuring movies, a franchise that is still very active. As for Gunn, those close to him note he’s somewhat relieved to go fully back to the creative side of the business. In an Instagram post on Monday, he wrote that executive life and the studio politics that surrounded it wasn’t always for him: “I will miss the people around me, and I will miss being the co-caretaker of these great characters, but I’m also incredibly relieved and excited to get back to pure filmmaking.” Latcham is currently untangling himself from projects he was producing, including the big budget movie Naruto for Lionsgate and Sony. By the time the news went public, Latcham and Gunn had not spoken about the DC transition, but were planning to speak by phone on Monday afternoon, according to sources. It is unclear if Gunn will get the chance to finish any of his vision for Superman, let alone the DC slate he and Safran announced with great fanfare in 2022 — a slate that was just barely revving up in the eyes of some. For DC fans, Monday’s tumult was another reminder how the franchise cannot catch a break in the 21 st century. At this stage, the only movies on the horizon are Man of Tomorrow and The Batman Part II , which recently saw Steven Soderbergh step behind the camera to help Matt Reeves. Whether or not fans will continue to invest in movies and actors before the rug is pulled out yet again is a real concern, said one source with knowledge of DC’s inner workings. item.title: In a nail-biter Senate race, incumbent Cindy Hyde-Smith stays out of view in Mississippi
item.description:
Source: Yahoo Top Stories (World)
Democratic Senate candidate Scott Colom, left, and GOP Sen. Cindy Hyde-Smith, right. - Rogelio V. Solis/Bill Clark/CQ-Roll Call, Inc./Getty Images As the Mississippi Senate race still remains too close to call, Democrat Scott Colom and GOP Sen. Cindy Hyde-Smith have taken completely different approaches towards the public. Since Election Day, Colom has held at least eight events and capitalized on the national attention of the race to flood the airwaves and make his case for why Democrats should no longer count out a state historically considered a Republican stronghold. Meanwhile, Hyde-Smith has not been seen publicly since she left her election night watch party just outside of Jackson after declaring that she would remain her state’s junior senator. While Colom has appeared at local universities, a Black-owned bookshop, a vinyl record store, a diner, and a senior citizens center and sat for multiple interviews with the media, Hyde-Smith has made her statements solely on X, including posting a Bible verse about hope on Sunday. “Ultimately, at some point, the senator needs to speak out. Where is Cindy Hyde-Smith?” Colom told reporters on Friday at the senior citizens facility in Jackson. “We want to hear from her. She needs to answer questions. What is her path to victory? She doesn’t have one.” Hyde-Smith’s campaign manager Jake Monssen said in a statement to CNN, “Senator Hyde-Smith and our team are working around the clock across Mississippi to protect the integrity of this election and to ensure every legal vote is counted.” As the Senate returned to session on Monday after a six-week recess, Hyde-Smith repeatedly declined to answer questions from reporters in the Capitol hallways about her election. “We’re still counting votes,” she eventually said as reporters trailed her through the building. Hyde-Smith did not answer when asked if she’ll go to court for a recount if she ultimately loses. Asked if she was surprised by the results of the race, the senator said she was surprised by the reporters following her. The divergent strategies speak to a dynamic that played out across the country this election cycle where Republicans in GOP strongholds like Hyde-Smith, who did not work to get ahead of the worsening national political landscape, were caught flatfooted and now find themselves in a once-unthinkable position. Now, Colom leads the incumbent senator by 2,500 votes in a race that could come down to thousands of provisional ballots, which election officials will vet in the coming days. If he wins, he will be Mississippi’s first Democratic senator in nearly four decades and its first Black senator since the Reconstruction era. Hyde-Smith’s campaign refused Colom’s invitations to debate prior to Election Day and did relatively few campaign events even as Colom was frequently on the trail and appearing with top Democrats like Kamala Harris and Bill Clinton. Even some of Hyde-Smith’s supporters have noticed their senator’s absence and how Colom has filled that void. A sign supporting Republican Sen. Cindy Hyde-Smith at a gas station in Brandon, Mississippi, on November 8, 2026. - Ellen Schmidt/AP John, an insurance adjuster from Hyde-Smith’s hometown of Brookhaven who declined to disclose his last name, is disappointed the Republican senator did not win in a landslide. Describing his community as the buckle to the Bible Belt, a county where Hyde-Smith outperformed Colom nearly 2:1, it’s hard for him to picture his home state turning blue. But John said he wished Hyde-Smith matched the television ads that he was inundated by from the Colom campaign. “I would like to personally have seen more campaigning from Cindy,” he told CNN. “I would like to have seen more ads for Cindy and put her name out there a little more. And it may be because she’s an incumbent and maybe didn’t feel like the need was there. I’m not sure. I don’t know.” For F.B. Warren, who has served on school boards with Hyde-Smith, Colom’s campaign should be a wakeup call for Republicans about how to not take Mississippi for granted. “It’s kind of like the team that plays a game of football, baseball, basketball, and they never have competition,” Warren told CNN. “So, in Mississippi and across the country, from the Republican Party standpoint, they got pushed. They now got pushed, so they’re going to have to get better. They’re going to have to campaign better. They’re going to have to have better candidates. They’re going to have to work harder, and that’s the big wake-up call.” His wife, Angie Warren, who owns two small stores in Hyde-Smith’s hometown, reflected on how Democrats did more to capitalize on voter enthusiasm this election season. “I do think that the Democratic Party has a better turnout for elections than the Republican Party. I don’t know why that is. I don’t know if they speak closer to the people and they get out and vote more. But for some reason, the Republican Party doesn’t always have the voter turnout that it needs,” she told CNN. While Mississippi has long been Republican territory, Colom and other Democrats have argued that the headwinds against the party in power and the state’s significant Black electorate made the state fertile ground for a flip this cycle. Further, Hyde-Smith, who was first appointed to the Senate in 2018, underperformed Republicans in 2020 as well, winning a full term by 10 points even as Trump won the state by 16. Democratic candidate for Senate Scott Colom speaks to reporters during a campaign event at the Tougaloo Senior Citizens Center in Jackson, Mississippi, on November 6, 2026. - Ellen Schmidt/AP The early lack of national attention to the race gave Colom a long runway to capitalize on Hyde-Smith’s uneven campaign performance. It wasn’t until late October that the Senate Leadership Fund, the leading GOP super PAC focused on Senate races, made an initial reservation of about $160,000 in Mississippi, according to AdImpact data. That reservation was in response to Senate Democrats announcing that they would spend r oughly $1 million on ads for the race. By that time, Colom had started to galvanize the party behind what was once considered a long-shot bid in a state Trump won two years ago by 23 points. Hyde-Smith has posted on social media since Election Day, including a statement on November 6 stating, “we are not backing down. This election is not over” and vowing to “see this through to the very end!” Mississippi GOP Chair Michael Hurst held a press conference last week to tout the 50-plus volunteer attorneys and observers Republicans had sent across the state, with many more are prepared to jump in to help. “Our attorneys and observers will continue to be in different parts of Mississippi – watching as election commissioners review and process these outstanding ballots, ensuring that our elections are followed and that only ballots which have been legally cast are counted,” he said. unknown content item - Even as both sides prepare for a potential legal battle over the results, Democrat Phillip Rollins told CNN that Colom’s nonstop style channeled the frustration that he and others were feeling in the lead up to the election. “People are fed up,” Rollins, who owns the comic book and record shop where Colom recently campaigned, said. “They need to see the change happen during their lifetime and not have to wait.” This story has been updated with additional details. CNN’s Lauren Fox and Manu Raju contributed to this report. item.title: Inflation data comes in hotter than expected, even as energy inflation fades
item.description:
Source: Yahoo Top Stories (World)
Consumer Price Index data for October showed that inflation remains elevated, as costs rose across a wide range of essential goods and services, including food, rent, and medical care. The Consumer Price Index rose 0.4% in October from a month earlier, higher than the 0.3% economists were expecting but below September's 0.6% gain, according to Labor Department data released on Tuesday. "Core" inflation, which strips out volatile food and energy prices, rose 0.3%, coming in ahead of the 0.2% economists were expecting to match September's level. October's report didn't include annual inflation figures because the Bureau of Labor Statistics was unable to publish full October 2025 data due to the government shutdown last year. But many economists estimate that inflation accelerated on a year-over-year basis. Read more: How to protect your savings against inflation Housing costs were a major contributor to October's price increases. Owners' equivalent rent, which measures homeownership costs, rose 0.3%, while rents were up 0.2%. Food costs were up 0.5%, driven by higher meat and dairy prices. Lettuce prices rose 7.3%, and baby food jumped 5.1%. Transportation costs accelerated 0.8% last month, while medical care items were up 0.5% and medical services rose 0.3%. "One hopes inflation starts returning to normal, but that's a hope right now, not a reality," economist Justin Wolfers wrote on X . Sale signs of meat are displayed on a refrigerated case inside a grocery store in Chicago, Thursday, June 25, 2026. (AP Photo/Nam Y. Huh) AP Photo/Nam Y. Huh Rising energy prices weighed heavily on September's report , but October's price increases were less dramatic. Energy costs rose 0.7% last month, down from 5.2% in September. "CPI for October is not great," Kevin Gordon, head of macro research and strategy at the Schwab Center for Financial Research, wrote in a post on X . "Inflation breadth still looking poor across goods and services," he wrote in another post, referring to the wide variety of categories in which prices are rising. Tuesday's inflation data is the Federal Reserve's final look at the CPI before it meets Dec. 8-9, although it will get another look at inflation data via its preferred measure, the Personal Consumption Expenditures index, later this month. The hot report, coupled with a labor market that's holding up and even showing signs of accelerating, cemented traders' expectations for a rate hike in December. Traders now see a 15.3% chance of a larger 50 basis point move . Claire Boston is a senior reporter for Yahoo Finance covering housing, mortgages, and home insurance. Aircraft and other assets move regularly ​according to operational ​requirements." Using public tracking site Flightradar24 BBC Verify has been able to see USAF KC-135 Stratotanker refuelling aircraft leaving Mildenhall throughout Monday. Two aircraft that left initially flew to US bases in Germany and Italy. The first KC-135 then returned to Mildenhall before heading east and landing at Spangdahlem airbase in Germany. The other aircraft - having flown circuits over Aviano airbase in Italy - flew on to and landed at Spangdahlem. Flight-tracking data also shows eight other US KC-135s left Mildenhall later on Monday. The prime minister's official spokesperson said "the protection of our bases, both in the UK and across the world, is a top priority, we work closely with the police and our allies to protect our sites". The BBC has found there is currently very little aircraft movement at the base, and there appears to be no additional security in place around it. The spaces from which the public can photograph aircraft remain open. The base is mostly used for refuelling and maintenance operations. Flights carrying US presidents, including Donald Trump, have often used it, and Trump transited through RAF Mildenhall on his way back to the US from the Nato summit in Ankara in July. US President Donald Trump walks across the tarmac at RAF Mildenhall in July [Getty Images] It has also been used as a staging area for aircraft and material bound for the Middle East. Air refuelling tankers were "forward deployed" to the region during operations against Iran. She added that "we take the security and safety of our bases incredibly seriously" and "we will always act on security intelligence when we need to". Due to operations security, we will not provide further information on movement of assets," the spokesperson added. Of course, they are large targets, an airbase has a long perimeter, so they are inevitably vulnerable." He added: "Nobody knows at this stage what this information was. I suspect part of it is an abundance of caution." Aircraft left RAF Mildenhall in Suffolk and landed at other American bases in Europe and also at Prestwick Airport in Ayrshire [Reuters] Speaking before reports emerged of the flights leaving RAF Mildenhall, US Secretary of State Marco Rubio was asked on Monday about Iranian threats against American diplomats overseas. item.title: Police contacted by 'several' people about Russell Brand after his rape conviction
item.description:
Source: Yahoo Top Stories (World)
A police force in the U.K. said Tuesday it has been contacted by "several people" about possible criminal allegations against disgraced comedian and actor Russell Brand, who was sentenced Monday to more than 10 years in prison for rape and sexual assaults. In a statement, London's Metropolitan Police said that "several people have contacted the investigation team during and since the trial to provide information or report a potential criminal allegation.” "Detectives are assessing this information as part of their ongoing enquiries," the police force added. Last week, Met Police commissioner Mark Rowley said that two further rape allegations were being investigated. On Monday, Metropolitan Police Detective Superintendent Andy Furphy appealed outside the court after Brand's sentencing for other potential accusers to come forward. Brand has not been charged regarding these new allegations. "I want to make a direct appeal to anyone who has been a victim of rape or any other sexual offense. We know it can take enormous courage to speak about what has happened to you, no matter how long ago it occurred or who was responsible," Furphy said outside of Southwark Crown Court. "If you come forward, you will be listened to, supported and treated with care and compassion." The statement follows allegations from Brand's former girlfriend, Jemima Goldsmith, who accused him of "violence, coercive control and abuse" while the two were together. In a statement shared on X , the TV producer, who dated Brand for a year, wrote that she had to call the police to have him removed from her house in 2014 "during a violent incident." She said that she has "neither seen nor spoken to Brand" since that period. "I chose not to press charges at the time and not to go public with this, as I was worried about the impact of the press attention on my then teenage children," she wrote. Brand was sentenced to 10 years and six months in prison Monday for raping a woman and sexually assaulting three more. The comedian is expected to serve at least two-thirds of that sentence — around seven years — before being eligible for release. Handing down the sentence at Southwark Crown Court in London, Judge Joel Bennathan said Brand told a series of lies throughout the trial, adding he had displayed a "casual and arrogant disregard" for women who said 'No' to him. "About 20 years ago, Russell Brand, you were becoming famous," Bennathan said. "You were clever — and in many people's eyes, funny and charismatic. You had also become a sexual predator." He added, "Whatever women wear, wherever they go, indeed whatever they drink, they retain the right to say 'no' and to demand justice from criminal courts when sexual predators like you, Russell Brand, act without their consent." Brand was supported in court by his wife, Laura, and his father, Ron. He is expected to serve at least two-thirds of that sentence — around seven years — before being eligible for release. Brand was found guilty of one count of rape and three counts of sexual assault on Nov. 5. He was acquitted of two rape counts and one count of attempted indecent assault. Prosecutor Riel Karmy-Jones called Brand a ruthless, calculating and manipulative "sexual predator" who treated women as a "disposable commodity." "Mr. Brand abused the influence and power that came with his fame," Karmy-Jones said. "He used it to facilitate an access to women without which the offending could not have taken place. It also fed his own view that he could commit such offenses with impunity." Ahead of his sentencing, one woman, who was sexually assaulted by Brand in 2004 or 2005, told the court in her impact statement : "Russell Brand is a sexual predator who has no remorse." Another woman, who was raped by the comedian in 2009 after meeting him at a comedy show in London, said she was "living with trauma." She said his fame made it "difficult to escape reminders of what had happened," BBC reported . She said she was worried after the attack that she might have HIV, struggled to eat and sleep, took nearly three months off work and abandoned the career she had embarked upon. "Although the rape was 17 years ago, she still finds it affects her ability to form new friendships and to know when she can trust people," the judge said. A third woman who was assaulted by Brand while working on a Channel 4 documentary said that, following the attack, she felt like she had "lost my trust in people." Reflecting on the incident, she added: "I felt powerless in that moment." Last week, Megyn Kelly, the former Fox News host, reacted to Brand's conviction in disbelief. "I don't believe the charges, and I don't have to believe them just because a jury came through with the opposite conclusion," she said in a YouTube livestream . The next day, in a comment on X, Elon Musk described Brand's conviction for offenses nearly 20 years old as a " crazy legal standard ." England doesn't have a statute of limitations for rape or sexual assault. Laura Brand, the wife of British actor and comedian Russell Brand, arrives at Southwark Crown Court on Nov. 9. REUTERS / REUTERS Brand became a household name in the U.K. in the 2000s as a comedian and broadcaster and had well-documented issues with drugs and alcohol. He went on to star in the movies Get Him to the Greek in 2010 and Arthur the following year. He married singer Katy Perry in October 2010, but Brand filed for divorce in December 2011, citing irreconcilable differences. Their divorce was finalized in July 2012. The claims against Brand were made by six different women, spanning from 1999 to 2009. None of the women knew each other, but came forward to police following a TV documentary and press reports in 2023, in which anonymous allegations were made by other women. During the trial, the court heard tearful testimony from the six accusers, who are all entitled to lifelong anonymity. According to the Associated Press, the convictions included a rape that took place in 2009, involving a woman who went to Brand's home after meeting him at one of his shows. She said she had engaged in consensual sex, but that Brand then raped her and removed a condom in the process. Brand was also convicted of sexually assaulting a woman when he grabbed her breasts at a London bar in 2004. He was also found guilty over an incident in 2009, in which he demanded a woman give him a massage in front of two of his colleagues and then put his head in her groin. A third complaint of sexual assault ended in a guilty verdict when Brand was found guilty of pushing a woman who worked at a radio station up against a wall and forcibly kissing her. Brand denied the charges and said he had never forced anyone to do something against their will. Footage released by London's Metropolitan Police Service after the verdict shows Brand being interviewed by police in December 2023. "As I've repeatedly stated publicly and written about extensively, I led a very promiscuous life in the past, which I've spent years openly denouncing," Brand can be seen saying. "I've never engaged in non-consensual sexual activity." He said he did "not recall the names" of the complainants, or meeting them, adding, "However, it's entirely possible that I may have encountered them and we may have engaged in consensual sexual activity or physical contact that's been since reimagined." Following the verdict, the Metropolitan Police Service told Yahoo that Brand, 51, was facing further allegations of rape from two women. "The suspect has previously been interviewed under caution in connection with the allegations," the force said. Brand has not been charged in relation to these claims. Rowley, the head of the Met Police, has urged any other victims of Brand to contact the police. "There's two more rape allegations that we're looking at. We're encouraging anybody else to come forward if there's any other allegations," he told reporters on Nov. 6. He later said that he "wouldn't be surprised if many, many more come forward. … This shows that powerful people can be brought down so you are safe stepping forward and we will support and try and bring that person to justice." item.title: Ole Miss students accused of making racist gestures outside Black students' home
item.description:
Source: Yahoo Top Stories (World)
Officials at the University of Mississippi are investigating a video showing three white women outside a Black student's apartment Friday evening, with two of them allegedly making racist noises and gestures captured on Ring camera footage. "[T]he incident is being actively investigated by the appropriate university offices," Vice Chancellor Shawnboda Mead said in a statement Monday, in part, adding, "our staff have reached out to the students directly impacted to offer support, listen to their concerns, and connect them with available resources. We will continue to support them as we work through this process." "Every student deserves to feel safe, respected, and valued at the University of Mississippi. Racism and actions that disparage people because of an aspect of their identity have no place in our campus community," the statement also said. The two women in the video, which was posted to TikTok, are seen briefly stepping toward the door camera, beating their chests while grunting and cooing like monkeys. The third woman glanced towards the camera, but she did not appear to make any gestures or monkey noises. The school said in its statement that it was investigating "the incident." The video had been viewed over 12 million times as of early Monday afternoon. Courtesy Jakiyra Metcalf - PHOTO: Ole Miss University is investigating video appearing to show students making monkey sounds and gestures, allegedly targeting Black students with racist tropes. The incident has sparked outrage online, with many comments decrying the video's apparent use of the racist trope of comparing Black people to monkeys. "The university is aware of a video depicting offensive, hurtful, and unacceptable behaviors that conflict with our university values and we condemn them," Ole Miss told ABC News in a statement. "The university has reached out to those targeted by the actions to share information, resources, and support." The school confirmed to ABC News that the women in the video are students at the university. It did not respond to ABC News' question regarding whether disciplinary action was taken against the students in the video. MORE: 'Racist' actions from counterprotesters at University of Mississippi prompt investigation "It's important to note that student conduct cases, records, and any potential disciplinary action are protected by the Family Educational Rights and Privacy Act (FERPA)," university representatives told ABC News. Jakiyra Metcalf, one of the Black students who lives in the apartment, told ABC News that they were expected to meet with university officials on Monday. Metcalf posted the video to TikTok over the weekend. "What do we have to say about this ??" she wrote in her post, tagging Ole Miss. Tasha Bolton, whose daughter is of one of the Black students living in the apartment, told ABC News that the women seen in the video live upstairs in the same apartment building. "The video has been shared with university administration, and we want answers. Specifically, what steps will be taken to address this behavior and ensure accountability?" Bolton posted online . "This is absolutely disgusting and unacceptable. College is supposed to be a place where young adults can learn, grow, and feel safe." Stacy Revere/Getty Images - PHOTO: The exterior of Vaught-Hemingway Stadium, Oct. 19, 2013 in Oxford, Mississippi. A similar incident occurred at the university in 2024 when a white student directed monkey gestures at a Black woman protesting the war in Gaza. That act was also captured on video. "As a public institution, we are committed to supporting the rights of our students, faculty, and employees to express their views in a respectful manner and to assemble peacefully as guaranteed by the First Amendment," Chancellor Glenn F. Boyce said then in an email response to the incident. "However, some individuals at the demonstration acted in ways that conflict with our university's values. Behaviors and comments that demean people because of their race or ethnicity marginalize them and undermine the values that are fundamental to a civil and safe society." The student who made the gestures toward the Black protester was ultimately expelled from his fraternity. ABC News' Rowan Henchy contributed to this report.
